content: Genital warts are a highly contagious sexually transmitted infection caused by specific subtypes of the human papillomavirus (HPV). The infection is transmitted through direct skin-to-skin contact during oral, genital, or anal sexual activity with an infected individual. Genital warts are the most visible clinical manifestation of genital HPV infection. They are primarily caused by HPV types 6 and 11, which are responsible for approximately 90% of cases. Other HPV strains, such as types 30, 42, 43, 44, 45, 51, 52, and 54, can also lead to genital warts, though less commonly. It is important to note that most individuals infected with these HPV strains do not develop warts or any other symptoms. While HPV is also a major cause of cervical cancer, the strains responsible for genital warts are distinct from those that cause cancer. Specifically, HPV types 16 and 18 are implicated in 70% of cervical cancer cases. Although treatments can effectively remove visible genital warts, they do not eradicate the underlying HPV infection. Consequently, warts may recur after treatment. Historically, it was believed that HPV persisted in the body indefinitely. However, recent studies utilizing advanced DNA detection techniques have demonstrated that the immune system can either clear the virus entirely or suppress it to levels undetectable by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing. According to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), approximately 70% of new HPV infections resolve within one year, and up to 91% clear within two years. The median duration of a new HPV infection is about eight months, with the immune system's gradual response likely playing a key role in viral clearance. The ability to clear the HPV virus is heavily influenced by the state of an individual's immune system. Factors such as HIV infection, immunosuppressive medications, stress, or other illnesses can impair the immune response and increase the likelihood of persistent infection. There is also evidence suggesting that effective treatment of genital warts may enhance the immune system's ability to combat the virus. Genital warts often present as clusters of small, flesh-colored growths, though they can vary in size and may coalesce into larger masses. In women, these warts can appear on the external and internal surfaces of the vagina, on the cervix, or around the anus. In men, warts are typically found on the tip of the penis but may also occur on the penile shaft, scrotum, or perianal region. In rare cases, genital warts can develop in the oral cavity or throat following oral sexual contact with an infected partner. In some cases, genital warts may resolve spontaneously without treatment. However, they can also persist and develop into raised, fleshy growths. It is impossible to predict whether warts will regress or progress over time. For small warts, treatment options include cryosurgery (freezing), electrocautery (burning), or laser therapy. Surgical excision may be necessary for larger warts that do not respond to other treatments. Primary prevention of genital warts and certain HPV-related cancers is possible through vaccination. The Gardasil vaccine, developed by Merck & Co., provides protection against HPV types 6, 11, 16, and 18. Types 6 and 11 are associated with genital warts, while types 16 and 18 are linked to cervical cancer. The vaccine is prophylactic, meaning it is designed to prevent infection and is not effective as a treatment for existing HPV infections. Gardasil is widely approved for use in young women and has also been approved for use in males in certain regions, such as the United Kingdom.
